name: Asparagus
summary: A long-lived perennial vegetable grown for its spring spears and feathery summer fern. The edible spears are shoots from an underground crown; leaving later shoots to fern is essential because the foliage replenishes reserves for future seasons. This species-level profile does not represent a named cultivar or a hydroponic crop.

UMN describes male and female plants as separate (dioecious); both produce edible spears, while female plants may set red, inedible berries. Some named hybrids are all-male, but this record does not imply a sex or hybrid cultivar.

cultivation.short: Permanent sunny site; deep roots need moist, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: UMN recommends a fertile, sunny, well-drained site that retains moisture, avoiding shallow or waterlogged ground and frost pockets. The planting may persist for 15 years or more. Its pH 6.5–7.0, bed preparation and row spacing are outdoor soil recommendations, not container dimensions, indoor light settings or hydroponic instructions. Tall mature ferns can shade nearby crops; the source suggests locating a bed at the north end of a larger garden in Minnesota.
items: Choose a sunny, fertile, well-drained permanent outdoor bed.
Plan space for deep perennial roots and vigorous summer fern growth.
Treat extension pH and spacing as soil-garden guidance, not hydroponic targets.

growth.short: Underground crowns produce spears that become energy-storing ferns
growth.guidance: UMN explains that edible spears are stems emerging from buds on the underground crown. Unharvested spears branch into tall, feathery foliage called fern; this foliage replenishes reserves used for the next year's crop. Spears can grow rapidly during peak season, so frequent observation matters. The crop is a persistent perennial, not a compact leafy green.
items: Recognize emerging spears as stems from the perennial crown.
Allow unharvested spears to develop into ferns that replenish the crown.

maintenance.short: After harvest, let the fern grow and keep it healthy
maintenance.guidance: Do not cut down green fern after the spear season: it builds reserves for the following year. UMN recommends removing fully brown, dormant old fern in late fall or early spring in its pest-management context; avoid removing it while still green. Maintain moisture during fern growth, control weeds carefully, and base fertilizer on a soil test rather than applying a fixed routine. Shallow cultivation is restricted because crowns and emerging spears can be damaged.
items: Protect green ferns after the harvest season.
Remove old fully dormant brown ferns only at the appropriate seasonal stage.
Keep the perennial bed weed-controlled and adequately watered.

flowering.short: Separate male and female plants; only female plants set berries
flowering.guidance: UMN Extension describes asparagus as dioecious. Both sexes produce edible spears; female plants can form red berries containing seed, while many named hybrids are all-male. Those differences belong to sex or specific variety identity and are not assigned to this cultivar-unspecified profile.

harvest.short: Cut spears at harvest size, then stop to restore crown reserves
harvest.guidance: In the Minnesota home-garden guide, allow crowns to establish before harvesting; a strong planting may begin in its second spring, while some gardeners wait until year three. UMN's commercial harvest guide gives 6–10 inches as a harvest size and describes a 6–8 week season for mature Minnesota stands; these are regional references, not a universal calendar. In the first picking year, limit harvest to about two weeks, then let spears fern. In later years, stop around the local season's end or when spears become pencil-thin / growth slows. Remove spears by snapping or cutting without injuring the crown; harvesting too long can weaken next year's crop.
items: Allow crowns to establish before starting regular harvest.
Select spears at an appropriate size for the local guide.
Stop harvest in time for healthy fern growth and crown recovery.

uses.short: Harvest young shoots as a spring vegetable; store promptly
uses.guidance: The edible portion is the young spear, used as a vegetable. UMN notes that freshly cut spears can be eaten soon after harvest and gives refrigeration, freezing and pressure-canning guidance for the home garden. Storage-life figures vary by source and handling, so this profile does not promise one universal shelf life. The later fern is important to plant health and is not the harvested vegetable.

problems.short: Recognize frost-damaged spears, beetle feeding and fern disease
problems.guidance: UMN notes that late spring frost can kill exposed spears. Common asparagus beetle larvae can make a spear curve into a shepherd's crook; dark eggs may be visible on spears or fern. On fern, rust can show cream-colored lesions or orange stripes, while Cercospora may cause tan/gray lesions with reddish borders and progressive yellowing. These are warning signs from Minnesota production guidance, not claims that every plant will be affected or that this species has resistance. Removing fully dormant old fern may reduce pest carryover; pesticide choices and legal labels are outside this general profile.

name: Rhubarb
summary: A long-lived, cold-hardy perennial grown for its tart edible leaf stalks, not its leaves. The plant forms a large crown and needs space, moisture and a long establishment period. Stalk color and vigor vary by variety; this profile does not represent a named cultivar.

cultivation.short: Sunny, well-drained garden site with room for a large crown
cultivation.guidance: UMN recommends full-day sun, moisture-retentive well-drained soil and a substantial garden area for each plant. Loam retains water and nutrients better than sand. In Minnesota garden soils, rhubarb tolerates a broad soil pH range; no hydroponic solution pH, container size or indoor-light requirement is inferred. Apply compost or fertilizer according to soil conditions and plant vigor, avoiding unnecessary phosphorus accumulation.
items: Choose a sunny outdoor bed with good drainage and room for the crown to expand.
Keep soil evenly supplied with moisture during active growth, without waterlogging.
Use soil conditions and plant vigor to decide whether compost or fertilizer is needed.

growth.short: Persistent crown produces large leaves and expanding stalk clusters
growth.guidance: Rhubarb is a long-lived perennial whose crown expands outward, forming buds for following seasons. A well-managed planting may live 15 years or more. Stalk color, length, fiber and vigor vary among varieties, so a species-level record cannot promise red stalks. The foliage is necessary for replenishing reserves after harvest.
items: Expect a perennial crown to persist while above-ground foliage changes seasonally.
Keep enough healthy foliage to rebuild crown reserves after the spring harvest.
Record seasonal growth and crown vigor rather than using stalk color alone as a maturity signal.
avoid: Interpreting a green-stalk cultivar as unripe solely because it is not red.

harvest.short: Twist-pull mature stalks; keep leaves out of food
harvest.guidance: Wait until the second growing season to harvest, or the third if the plant was started from seed. When stalks reach full length, grasp near the base, pull and twist rather than cutting at the crown. Trim and discard the leaf blades promptly because they are toxic. Minnesota guidance places the main harvest in spring to early summer; stop regular picking so remaining leaves replenish the crown. This is regional timing, not a universal harvest calendar.

maintenance.short: Water through summer, control weeds and divide aging crowns
maintenance.guidance: UMN recommends thorough watering during the growing season, including after harvest, and careful weed control while plants establish. Divide older crowns in early spring as growth begins if the center becomes less productive; each division needs viable buds. Remove emerging flower stalks to redirect resources to vegetative growth. Leave healthy leaves in place after harvest so the crown can rebuild reserves.

problems.short: Watch for waterlogging, crown rot and damaged or spotted foliage
problems.guidance: Poor drainage and wet conditions can promote root or crown rot. UMN describes rhubarb curculio and stalk borers as possible causes of holes in stalks or crowns, and Ascochyta or Ramularia as causes of leaf spots in Minnesota. Unusual leaf color and declining vigor may have several causes, including viruses; symptoms alone do not establish a diagnosis. Remove fully dead foliage after hard frost where appropriate; avoid treating all leaf spotting as one disease.

uses.short: Cook the tart stalks; never use the leaves as food
uses.guidance: The edible portion is the leaf petiole (stalk), typically cooked and sweetened for pies, sauces, cakes, preserves or drinks. Green and red stalks can both be edible; red color does not establish sweetness. The leaf blades are toxic and must be discarded. The roots are not part of the edible harvest.

name: Escarole
summary: A broad-leaved form of endive grown as a salad and cooking green. It shares crop-level culture with other chicories, while its broad, smoother leaves distinguish it from curly endive.

identity.short: Accepted species: Cichorium endivia; broad-leaved escarole type
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Cichorium endivia. UMN Extension distinguishes escarole as a broad, smooth-leaved form of endive and curly endive as another type; this record does not name a cultivar.
identity.context: This advice is limited to the cited species, crop or product scope; check local climate and cultivar.

cultivation.short: Cool-season chicory culture; keep shallow roots moist
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension groups escarole with chicories and describes them as cool-season crops. Its Minnesota guide gives a 6.0–6.8 soil-pH range for lettuce and chicories and emphasizes well-drained, moisture-retentive soil because most water- and nutrient-absorbing roots are shallow. Treat these as regional garden-soil context, not solution pH or a hydroponic recipe; adapt dates to local climate.

Keep the shallow root zone adequately moist; dry soil can reduce growth and quality.

harvest.short: Use leaves as a salad or cooking green
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension notes that recipes usually use escarole cooked. Its chicory/leafy-green guidance supports harvesting usable outer leaves repeatedly while leaving most small inner leaves, or cutting the plant at or just above soil level for a whole-plant harvest. Frequent watering in the days before harvest can improve crispness; no cultivar-specific harvest date is assigned.

problems.short: Heat, dry soil and bolting can reduce quality
problems.guidance: UMN reports that chicories perform best in cool conditions and that heat and long days can trigger bolting, which ends leaf harvest and causes pronounced bitterness. The guide also describes tipburn (browned leaf edges) when watering resumes after a dry spell. These are crop-group warning signs in a Minnesota guide, not cultivar-specific resistance claims.

Brown leaf edges after watering resumes from a dry spell may be tipburn; aim for steadier soil moisture.
Inspect leaves for chewing holes and young plants for cutworms; the guide also identifies slugs/snails and flea beetles in these crops.

maintenance.short: Optional blanching can produce a paler heart
maintenance.guidance: UMN describes tying the outer leaves of endive around the heart to blanch inner leaves; the process takes about two weeks, and close spacing may partly self-blanch plants. Since escarole is a broad-leaved endive type, this is a type-level technique a grower may choose, not a requirement or cultivar-specific result.
